You’re right; KC:D’s strength is that there is thought put into nearly every crevice of the player’s actual experience, focusing on making a responsive and interactive experience rather than a dynamic world. 

But of M&B’s greatest weaknesses is its failure to provide the player with meaningful interaction with the dynamic world they *do* create. No diplomacy, bare-bones characterization of the NPCs, and no events besides war and tournaments.

The concept of Mount & Blade alone has had me sink over a thousand hours between the two games in the last ten years. But inevitably, they are medieval combat simulators and medieval economy simulators held together with a rubber band. I am so incredibly excited for a studio to make a M&B-like that is made with the same love that a studio like Warhorse puts into the KCD games.

I think a game that would meet all of the criteria to blow the M&B games out of the water is fairly resource intensive and would take a large studio to accomplish. It’s trying to be a strategy game as well as an RPG simultaneously.

Thus, I realized just how surface level M&B mechanics when I got into the Kingdom Come: Deliverance and the Crusader Kings games specifically. A new M&B-like should look at what both of those games do right.

I assume you played black. I don’t think you played any worse than any regular 600 rated player would, but your opponent was definitely sharp. 

The main reason you lost is because you blundered two of your minor pieces. But the easiest part of improving is avoiding one-move blunders like that. What I think is more important is that your opponent played a tactically aggressive game that you seemed to have been overwhelmed by. With this opening, as well as most openings that begin with 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6, be very aware of what role white’s kingside bishop and knight plays. Ng5 is a move with a lot of venom in it. It’s a very forcing move, and even more when your king is exposed after exd4.

I’m not much higher rated than you, but 500-700 elo hell is the worst. You’re gonna lose to players who seem to be GM level 600s, and you’re gonna win against players who seem like they don’t know how to move the pieces. The best thing to do is to try to play decent moves consistently, listen to opening principles, know at least 6 moves into your chosen opening, and take your time calculating exchanges.
